_: The Night Library canon — stories chosen because a child who hears them inherits something: a bigger imagination, a template for resilience, and pride in what humans have done and can do. Each seed carries a 'truth' note so the parent can answer 'did that really happen?'

seeds.title: The King Who Learned to Have a Friend
seeds.hook: The oldest story humans ever wrote down is about a king who was too strong, and the wild man who became his best friend.
seeds.truth: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest surviving great work of literature, pressed into clay tablets four thousand years ago.

seeds.title: The Leap Across the Sea
seeds.hook: Hanuman had forgotten he could fly — until a friend needed him on the far side of the ocean.
seeds.truth: In the Ramayana, Hanuman's powers return only when someone reminds him who he is. The story is told to children across South and Southeast Asia.

seeds.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
seeds.hook: The spider who tried to keep all the wisdom in the world inside one pot — and what his small son taught him.
seeds.truth: Anansi stories traveled from Ghana across the Atlantic and survived everything; they became Br'er Rabbit in America. Stories are cargo that cannot be confiscated.

seeds.title: The Boy Who Slowed the Sun
seeds.hook: The days were too short for anyone to finish their work, so Māui braided a rope strong enough to catch the sun.
seeds.truth: Māui is the great trickster-hero of Polynesian navigators — people who crossed the largest ocean on Earth reading stars and waves, with no instruments.

seeds.title: Nobody Escapes the Giant
seeds.hook: Trapped in a cave by a one-eyed giant, the cleverest sailor alive saved his crew with a fake name and a flock of sheep.
seeds.truth: Homer's Odyssey was sung for centuries before it was written. 'Nobody' is still the best trick in literature.

seeds.title: The Man Who Caught Words
seeds.hook: Sequoyah could not read any language — so he spent twelve years inventing a way to write his own, and gave it to every Cherokee child.
seeds.truth: Sequoyah created the Cherokee syllabary alone, one of the only writing systems in history invented by a single person. Within years, Cherokee literacy surpassed that of their neighbors.

seeds.title: Twelve Seconds in the Wind
seeds.hook: Two brothers who fixed bicycles believed they could fly. The first flight lasted twelve seconds — shorter than this sentence takes to read aloud.
seeds.truth: The Wright Flyer flew 120 feet at Kitty Hawk. Sixty-six years later, humans stood on the Moon. One lifetime.

seeds.title: The Girl Who Dreamed a Thinking Machine
seeds.hook: A hundred years before computers existed, Ada wrote about a machine that could weave numbers the way looms weave flowers.
seeds.truth: Ada Lovelace wrote the first published algorithm — for a computer that was never built. She saw what it could become before anyone else did.

seeds.title: The Ship That Came Home
seeds.hook: Three astronauts, a broken ship, and a room full of people on the ground who refused to stop solving the problem.
seeds.truth: Apollo 13's crew survived on the lunar module's air and the ground crew's arithmetic. 'Failure is not an option' became a human inheritance.

seeds.title: The Longest Walk in the World
seeds.hook: A young man left home for a pilgrimage and didn't stop traveling for twenty-nine years — three times farther than Marco Polo.
seeds.truth: Ibn Battuta crossed 44 modern countries and dictated his Rihla from memory. The world has always been connected by the curious.

seeds.title: The Woman Who Planted a Forest
seeds.hook: When the rivers dried and the firewood ran out, Wangari did not write a law. She planted a tree. Then thirty million more.
seeds.truth: Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement won her the Nobel Peace Prize — the first for connecting peace to the soil itself.

seeds.title: The Teacher of Alexandria
seeds.hook: In the city with the greatest library on Earth, the most famous teacher was a woman who mapped the stars and asked her students to question everything.
seeds.truth: Hypatia taught mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy to students of every faith. Libraries burn; the habit of asking does not.
